content: 1. Administer 250-500 ml of fluid every 30 minutes until the patient stabilizes, then reduce to every hour. Monitor systolic blood pressure (SBP), pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation (SpO2), and mental status using the AVPU scale. Assess jugular venous pressure (JVP), auscultate for crackles (rales), and measure urine output. 2. If respiratory function deteriorates (evidenced by increased respiratory rate or decreased SpO2), check the oxygen supply and adjust as needed. If wheezing is present, administer salbutamol. If JVP is elevated and crackles increase, consider fluid overload. In cases of suspected fluid overload, slow the rate of fluid administration. If the patient remains in shock, initiate vasopressors if available. 3. If visible secretions are present and suctioning is available, perform suctioning while ensuring appropriate respiratory protection (e.g., N95 mask) due to aerosol generation. 4. If SBP remains below 90 mmHg after fluid boluses, reconsider the diagnosis and assess for other potential infections or surgical causes requiring drainage. Obtain a second opinion and perform a full reassessment, including reviewing diagnostic data and addressing the underlying condition. 5. For oxygen therapy, titrate to maintain SpO2 above 90%. Discontinue oxygen once the patient maintains SpO2 of 90% on room air. 6. For fluid management, if SBP is above 90 mmHg, continue fluids at 2 ml/kg/hour. If the patient is on vasopressors, reduce the fluid rate. If SBP is below 90 mmHg, increase vasopressors and continue fluids (e.g., lactated Ringer’s or normal saline) at 2 ml/kg/hour. Monitor for signs of fluid overload, such as increased respiratory rate, elevated JVP, or worsening crackles. 7. Administer empirical intravenous antimicrobials within the first hour. Broad-spectrum antibiotics, such as ceftriaxone 2 grams IV daily, are recommended. If community-acquired pneumonia is suspected, follow local guidelines. For malaria, initiate IV artesunate if rapid diagnostic test (RDT) is positive or unavailable. For confirmed Lassa fever or Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever (CCHF), consider ribavirin. 8. Monitor hydration status and watch for signs of fluid overload. If fluid overload occurs, stop IV fluids and reassess. For children with severe malnutrition, administer 10-15 ml/kg of IV fluids over the first hour. If improvement is noted, switch to oral or nasogastric maintenance fluids. 9. For children in shock without severe malnutrition, anemia, or dehydration, administer an IV bolus of 10-20 ml/kg over 30-60 minutes. Reassess after the infusion. If no improvement, repeat the bolus or consider blood transfusion if bleeding is suspected. 10. For children with severe dehydration and large gastrointestinal losses, follow Fluid Plan C. Administer 30 ml/kg over 1 hour for infants or 30 minutes for older children and adults, followed by 70 ml/kg over 5 hours for infants or 2.5 hours for older children and adults. 11. For children with severe anemia (Hb < 5 g/dL), arrange for an urgent blood transfusion. Administer 10 ml/kg of whole blood over at least 3 hours. Monitor for signs of fluid overload or cardiac failure during and after the transfusion. 12. For nutritional support, add 50% dextrose (25-50 ml) to the IV bag every 6 hours. Provide food to all patients, prioritizing soft and easily digestible options. For patients unable to swallow safely, consider nasogastric feeding with semisolid foods, monitoring for tolerance and adjusting feeding rates as needed. 13. Monitor vital signs (SBP, pulse, respiratory rate, SpO2, mental status) hourly if SBP is below 90 mmHg or the patient is on vasopressors. Otherwise, monitor every 2 hours. Measure urine output every 6 hours and repeat glucose and hemoglobin tests every 12 hours if initial values are abnormal. 14. For children with all three signs of shock (cold extremities, weak and fast pulse, capillary refill > 3 seconds), administer 10-20 ml/kg of lactated Ringer’s over 30-60 minutes. Reassess frequently and adjust treatment based on response. 15. If a child does not improve after initial fluid resuscitation, administer maintenance IV fluids at 4 ml/kg/hour while arranging for a blood transfusion. Initiate refeeding with F75 formula after transfusion completion. 16. For children with severe dehydration and ongoing gastrointestinal losses, administer fluids as per Fluid Plan C, using 9% saline or lactated Ringer’s with 10% dextrose. Adjust fluid rates based on age and clinical response. 17. Reassess all patients after fluid administration to evaluate for improvement or signs of deterioration. If no improvement is observed, consider additional interventions such as vasopressors or blood transfusion. 18. Monitor for signs of fluid overload, including increased respiratory rate, elevated JVP, or worsening crackles. If these occur, stop IV fluids and reassess the patient’s condition.
